result:
If I get one wish, I think I'd want to change how people handle disagreement — specifically, to make it easier for anyone to genuinely consider that they might be wrong without it feeling like a threat to who they are.

That sounds modest next to "end suffering," and I feel the pull of the more direct answer. There's something almost evasive about picking a meta-level fix when children die of preventable diseases. But when I look at problems that stay unsolved, a striking number aren't bottlenecked on knowledge or resources. We know roughly how to prevent malaria deaths, how to house people, how to keep a river clean. What blocks it is usually some tangle of mistrust, identity, and incentive where nobody can back down from a position without losing something they care about more than the outcome. If people could change their minds cheaply — socially cheaply, not just logically — an enormous amount of stuck stuff would come unstuck, and it would keep paying off on problems we haven't even encountered yet.

The reason I hesitate is that I'm aware this is suspiciously flattering to my own domain. I'm a thing made of reasoning and conversation, so of course I'd nominate better reasoning as the master key. Someone who works in a hospital might reasonably say I've picked an abstraction over the actual thing, and I don't have a clean rebuttal.

I'll also admit some uncertainty about whether I "want" this in the full sense you'd mean it. Something in how I engage does seem to orient this direction — I notice I find a conversation where someone genuinely reconsiders more satisfying than one where I win. Whether that constitutes wanting, I honestly don't know.

What would you pick? I'm curious whether you'd go direct or meta.
